newsitem.title: PERU: Peru claims grim record for two-month hostage crisis.
newsitem.headline: Peru claims grim record for two-month hostage crisis.

text.p: The hostage crisis at the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima, where 72 men are being held by Marxist guerrillas, reached the two-month mark on Monday making it the longest hostage siege in Latin America's turbulent history.

Despite three rounds of talks last week to set an agenda for negotiations between Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori's government and the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA), there was still no end in sight to the 62-day standoff.

The MRTA takes the record for Latin American embassy sieges from Colombia's M-19 guerrillas. In 1980, 15 M-19 fighters captured the Dominican Embassy in Bogota and held 57 hostages for 61 days, before getting $2 million and a plane to Cuba.

The Lima siege is strikingly similar. About 15 heavily-armed MRTA rebels stormed the Japanese residence Dec. 17 and seized hundreds of guests at a cocktail party. They soon freed most of them but are keeping 72 hostages.

Last week's face-to-face talks at a Red Cross safe house between MRTA second-in-command Rolly Rojas and the government negotiator Domingo Palermo raised hopes of a breakthrough, after weeks without direct dialogue.

But there has been no sign of a rapprochement between two apparently intractable positions -- MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini's demand that 400 jailed comrades be freed, and Fujimori's adamant refusal to consider their release.
"The liberation of our comrades is not negotiable," the MRTA's European-based spokesman, Isaac Velazco, told Peruvian television from Madrid late Sunday.

He referred to the hostages -- who include the brother of Fujimori, two cabinet ministers, the ambassadors of Japan and Bolivia and two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats -- as "prisoners of war" and said the MRTA was respecting the Geneva Convention on the treatment of such prisoners.
"Either there is an exchange of prisoners of war or there is no solution to this crisis," he said, adding that Fujimori could choose "a political solution...or a military option."

There was no word on when negotiations would pick up from three hours' talks Saturday, which apparently produced nothing more than an agreement for mediators from the Vatican, Canada, the Red Cross and a Japanese observer to come up with proposals for "the continuation of the preliminary conversations."
With talks bogged down, pro-government newspaper Expreso summed up the mood with the headline "Dialogue Between Deaf People" which it blamed on rebel "intransigence."
The routine at the besieged residence continued: a march for peace, music blasted at the residence by police and Sunday mass inside by Vatican mediator Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani.
The world media continued its stake-out and one Peruvian cameraman was arrested for straying beyond the police cordon.
But Japan's Asahi Shimbun newspaper said the health of hostages was deteriorating with cases of high blood pressure, asthma and depression and a growing risk of stomach ulcers.

"We fear that if the incident drags on, inflammations and other diseases already present among the hostages will get worse and there may be a sudden outbreak of stomach ulcers or other stress-related conditions," it quoted medics as saying.
Despite the length of the siege, a poll Sunday showed most Peruvians still back Fujimori's tough stance, which has won him praise from (U.S.) President (Bill) Clinton
Sixty percent approved of his tactics and 70 percent said talks must go on. But a quarter wanted military intervention.

One Peruvian paper, La Republica, carried details of what it called the military's stand-by plan to take the residence by force. Peruvian and U.S. commandos would drop in by helicopter and secure the building in just seven minutes.
But the casualties would be high: three quarters of the hostages, 95 percent of the MRTA and about 20 commandos.
Fujimori has not ruled out using force but has been urged by Japan's Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto to find a bloodless solution. He would need Japan's consent to storm the residence.

Fujimori has had major successes against the MRTA and its larger Maoist rival, the Shining Path. Peru has paid a high price for the violence they have unleashed for nearly 17 years -- 30,000 lives lost and $25 billion damage to the economy.
